summary.name: Reliable releases and rollbacks (CRE life lessons)
summary.one_liner: A Google Cloud Blog article by Google SRE engineer Adrian Hilton on detecting bad releases, rolling back safely, and planning releases so rollbacks stay low-risk.
use_cases: Planning a rollback procedure before shipping a new binary
Detecting when a new service release is causing errors
Deciding between rolling back and rolling forward during an outage
Designing database schema changes that stay compatible with rollbacks
Testing that rollbacks still work before they are needed
Structuring staged releases to limit user exposure to bugs
summary.what_it_does: The article argues that most outages come from new binary releases and that teams should assume every release may contain bugs. It describes three reliability tasks: detecting a broken release, moving users safely off it, and limiting exposure via canarying. It recommends breaking down error and latency metrics by release version to catch subtle failures. It advocates rolling back first rather than rushing a roll-forward fix, and suggests periodically testing rollbacks. For schema changes, it proposes a feature-free intermediate release (v+1) so binaries and schema can be rolled back independently. The piece ends by promising a follow-up on canarying.
notable: Recommends a feature-free release (v+1) before a schema change so rollbacks don't require reverting the schema
Advises testing rollbacks periodically when things are healthy, and treating a rollback as the default response to suspected bugs
Mentions Stackdriver monitoring and nginx load balancing as examples of its assumed setup
caveats: Covers general principles only; it does not describe specific tools beyond nginx and Stackdriver
Part 2 on canarying is referenced but not included on this page
